field_deviations.name: rulings-same-date-order
field_deviations.note: PRE-EXISTING, LANGUAGE-INDEPENDENT and already in the README's deviations list. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-16 and it does NOT close: the candidate fix was to preserve the rulings bulk file's row order within a date, on the theory that the dump is exported in internal-id order. Tested against api.scryfall.com over 25 cards that have both several dates and a date carrying 4+ rulings, the file's order matched 0 of 25 — as did that order reversed, whole-file order, date-ascending-then-file, and the comment rule this port ships. The reason is direct: the six shared 'kicker' rulings come back in a DIFFERENT order on different cards (Strength of Night, Goblin Barrage and Spell Contortion each get their own permutation of the same six comments), so Scryfall orders by a per-(card, ruling) row id rather than a per-ruling one, and the dump — one line per pair, grouped by card — cannot reproduce that within a card. So date desc + comment stays, and determinism is load-bearing beyond tidiness: identical bucket bytes are what let the publisher skip rewrites against the 1,000-writes/day budget. Both sides return the SAME 26 rulings for mom/230 in a different order; the array LENGTH is still compared (an array-length diff is not covered by this path), so a missing or extra ruling still fails. Nothing to do with the foreign id — /cards/<the English id>/rulings differs identically. rulings-en-jotun-grunt passes because that card has no crowded date.

known_deviation.reason:
THE ONE PREFIX THAT SEPARATES pg_trgm SIMILARITY FROM EVERY LENGTH METRIC IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is why it is pinned and `q=lig`, `q=ang`, `q=gob` and `q=sh` are not. 10fc323 (upstream #927 9df17a3) replaced upstream's `ORDER BY rank, length(card_name), card_name` with Postgres `pg_trgm` similarity — |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| over the 3-character windows of `"  " + s + " "`, computed on the COLLATED name. Length looked like the rule because with separators gone and no repeated window the denominator IS the collated length, so a prefix where the two agree proves nothing. This one disagrees twice, opposite ways:
  LONG BEATS SHORT. `Serra Avenger` is 12 collated characters and scores 4/13 = 0.3077; `Serenity` is 8 and scores 3/10 = 0.3000. Both sides put Avenger at data.4 and Serenity at data.5. `Serenity` is shorter by four characters and still loses, because a name ending in the query's tail shares the closing `er ` window and `Serenity` (…`ty `) does not — the intersection is 4 against 3.
  AND SHORT BEATS LONG AT THE SAME SCORE. `Serendib Sorcerer` is 16 collated characters and scores 4/16 = 0.2500, tying the 10-character `Serum Snare`, `Serpentine`, `Serra's Boon`, `Serra's Hymn` and `Serra Angel` at 3/12. A length key of any kind sorts a 16 against five 10s; similarity does not distinguish them at all.
So a silent regression to a length sort cannot pass this case in either direction, and that is the whole reason it exists.

THE SIMILARITY BLOCKS THEMSELVES AGREE EXACTLY, which is the assertion, and the residual is the same undecidable ordinal 10fc323 recorded. Measured against api.scryfall.com 2026-08-17: both sides return the SAME 20 names, and both partition them into the same eight score blocks in the same order — 0.3750 Seraph; 0.3636 Serum Raker; 0.3333 Serum Powder; 0.3077 {Serene Master, Serra Avenger}; 0.3000 Serenity; 0.2857 Serra Redeemer; 0.2727 Serum Tank; 0.2500 six names; 0.2308 six names. Every position through data.7 is a block of one and both sides agree on all eight of them. From data.8 the blocks have six members each and the order WITHIN a block differs: this port sorts a tie by printed name ascending, and Scryfall's order inside a tie is a fixed internal ordinal that 10fc323 proved underivable — over 1,121 tie-ordered pairs from 30 measured prefixes, 28 card features in both directions separate none of them and the lexicographic fixpoint over all 56 candidates returns the EMPTY KEY. data.9 agreeing on `Serpentine` is coincidence inside a tie and is not recorded.

WHAT EACH SIDE IS HELD TO. data.0/4/5/7 are recorded on BOTH sides and are the ordering statement — a length sort moves data.4 and data.5 past each other, a missing rank split or a collation change moves data.0. data.8/13/14 are recorded per side: 8 is the first divergence, 13 is the last member of the 0.2500 block and 14 the first member of the 0.2308 block, so a change that leaked a name ACROSS a block boundary reports as drift on both sides even though the within-block order is free. If Scryfall's data.8/13/14 move while the blocks hold, their internal ordinal moved and this recording is what says so.

cases.name: search-order-edhrec-desc-unranked-first

volatile_order.note: The two sides do not hold the same NUMBERS for this column, so `data` is compared by rule and not by position — see checkVolatileOrder in scripts/live-parity.ts for the four rules and why each one survives the churn.

cases.note:
THE ANCHOR FOR THE NULL-RANK PLACEMENT, and the one page where it is visible. `order=edhrec` is the DEFAULT orderby, and a missing EDHREC rank used to sort as the LOWEST value here — first ascending, last descending — because `perm_primary_key` gave every column one absent side. api.scryfall.com does the opposite for a RANK: this page leads with 33 unranked printings and then runs downward, while ascending page 1 holds no null at all in its 175 rows. Descending is the direction that fits the evidence on ONE page, which is why the case is `dir=desc`: ascending puts the nulls at the far end of 425 rows, three pages away, where a page-1 comparison would pass against either rule. Generation 37 rebuilt the stored permutation; before it, this page opened with our highest real rank (29937 in this store) where Scryfall opens with 33 unranked rows, so the two disagreed on the first 33 ids.

WHY IT IS `volatile_order` AND NOT A POSITIONAL COMPARISON. `edhrec_rank` is not merely volatile in VALUE — the two sides are ranking against DIFFERENT DUMPS, and the disagreement reaches the ORDER. Measured 2026-08-17: `Infernal Pet` is 25740 on api.scryfall.com and 25733 here, while `Runeforge Champion` is 25731 there and 25740 here. Each side is correctly sorted by its own numbers and the two pages still put the pair in opposite orders. All ten positional differences on that page were exactly this — four adjacent blocks, every one a pair the two snapshots rank in opposite directions — and Scryfall refreshes daily, so a position-for-position comparison fails forever with nothing to fix.

WHAT IS STILL PINNED, and it is more than the case asserted before: the 33-row unranked block id for id (which no snapshot skew can move, since an unranked row has no number to drift); that both sides are monotone descending in their OWN ranks; that every pair the two snapshots agree about strictly is ordered the same way by both pages (9,995 pairs asserted, 16 exempt on 2026-08-17); and — because the two `data` arrays are aligned by id before the byte comparison — every field of all 175 card objects, exactly as before. What is NOT asserted is the relative order of rows the two snapshots cannot separate, which is the only thing the churn can move and the only thing this case never meant to pin.

known_deviation.reason:
NOT AN ORDERING DEFECT, AND NOT A PARAMETER SCRYFALL IMPLEMENTS. Four sweep findings traced here; this entry closes them so nobody reinvestigates it as a sort bug.

THE EVIDENCE, measured 2026-08-17 in six serial requests to api.scryfall.com over `e:khm unique=prints` (425 rows). `order=cubecobra` is BYTE-IDENTICAL to `order=name` in BOTH directions — raw bodies equal, same 425 ids in the same sequence, and `next_page` on the cubecobra response carries `order=name`, not `order=cubecobra`.

AND THE FALLBACK IS NOT SPECIFIC TO `cubecobra`, which is the measurement that settles what to do about it. `order=elo` — a value invented for this test that no one documents — comes back byte-identical to both of them, 425 rows, `next_page` order=name, no warning. Meanwhile `order=review`, which Scryfall DOES document, answers a genuinely different order (Battlefield Raptor, Codespell Cleric, Usher of the Fallen) and echoes `order=review`. So api.scryfall.com does not accept `cubecobra` and decline to implement it: it does not RECOGNISE it, and silently coerces every unrecognised order to `name`, exactly as it does a typo.

THE DECISION IS TO KEEP OUR IMPLEMENTATION, deliberately, and the byte-identity above is why rather than why not.
  1. Matching the fallback would not be matching a documented Scryfall behaviour. It would be matching Scryfall's UNKNOWN-PARAMETER COERCION, which the `elo` probe shows is all this is.
  2. This route already implements that coercion. `order=elo` here answers 200 sorted by name, same as Scryfall. `cubecobra` diverges only because this project RECOGNISES the word. To match, the vocabulary would have to be made smaller on purpose — to forget a word it knows — and no rule in this repo asks for that.
  3. Parity's purpose is that a client written against api.scryfall.com gets the same answer here. No such client sends `order=cubecobra`: Scryfall neither documents it nor treats it as anything but a typo, so there is no reason for one to exist. The only caller who sends it is written against THIS project, and that caller wants the ordering.
  4. The cost is not zero. `cubecobra_score` is a corpus-global PERCENT_RANK over the distinct card names of the whole corpus (engine/wasm-import/src/lib.rs), stored as a column and sorted on. Matching the fallback would strand that pipeline to win byte-parity on a query nobody makes.
  5. And the asymmetry runs one way. A caller who wanted name order can ask for `order=name` and get byte-identical answers from both sides; a caller who wanted cubecobra order has no other way to ask.

`next_page` ECHOING `cubecobra` IS PART OF THE SAME DECISION, not a second one: page 1 comes back in cubecobra order, so a `next_page` that said `order=name` would page 2 by name and split one result set across two orderings. scripts/parity-sweep.ts classifies this UNSUPPORTED for the same reason.

ONE ADJACENT DIVERGENCE, RECORDED HERE AND NOT CHASED: on an order it does not recognise this route emits a `warnings` array ("Unrecognized order 'elo'; sorted by name instead.") where api.scryfall.com emits none. That is about UNKNOWN orders, not about `cubecobra`, and it is not what these four findings were.

WHAT EACH SIDE IS HELD TO. Scryfall's recording is its name-order answer, which is fully determined and cannot drift; if it ever stops matching `order=name`, Scryfall has started implementing something. Ours records that data.0 is NOT the name-order row. A change to `Village Rites` there is DRIFT, not a failure, and means the nightly cubecobra table moved — re-measure and re-record.

The one unique of the three that moves, and it moves by exactly one row: `khm/A-40`. Scryfall dedupes an artwork ACROSS cards, and A-Alrund carries Alrund's front and back illustrations unchanged, so its 26 printings collapse to 25 with the A-* row as the one that goes. This port's scope is PER-CARD — 5d86e76 made the key the whole face tuple, c7d8cf3 measured that dropping oracle_id from the scope reproduces both of Scryfall's numbers exactly (26 -> 25 here, 187 -> 174 on znr), and 5440875 deferred the change on purpose — so A-Alrund keeps an artwork of its own and this answers 26.
WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN FIXED: closing the scope needs a corpus-wide dense artwork id in place of `artwork_base[card] + gid`, a cross-partition dedupe in the gather (cross-card groups must be co-located in one partition to keep `unique=art` a per-partition row predicate, and today's partitioning is `fnv1a64/oracle_id/v1`), a deterministic tie-break on row identity that the per-card scope provably never needed, and a representative rule that search-unique-art-znr-creatures proves is not derivable at all. Sized on the served store it buys 102 cross-oracle groups over 417 rows.
WHAT EACH SIDE STILL PROVES: both sides lead with khm/15 in the same order and differ only from data.3 on, where Scryfall has already dropped A-40 and moved khm/50 up. The sibling cases pin `unique=cards` 13 and `unique=prints` 26 byte-clean, so a change in the 25 or the 26 here is the artwork rule and nothing else.

cases.name: search-usd-coalesce-is-on-the-search-key-not-the-column
cases.note:
THE ONLY CASE IN THIS FILE THAT CAN TELL THE `usd`/`eur` FIX FROM ITS PLAUSIBLE WRONG VERSION, and it needs a declaration to do it. 417bed6 (upstream #927 10a6fb7) put the foil/etched fallback on the SEARCH KEY — the filter, the printing-space range index, the `order=usd` sort key and the representative pick that feeds it — and deliberately NOT on the stored price column. All five printings here prove the first half by being in the answer at all: `fin/551`, `551a`, `551b`, `551c` and `551d` every one serve `"usd": null` and match `usd>=1000` on foil prices of $5,950.00, $1,790.64, $1,772.97, $1,917.02 and $1,901.26. api.scryfall.com returns the same five, same ids, same order.
WHY THE DECLARATION. Coalescing into the STORED column passes every count and every filter test in this repo and corrupts the card object on 12,865 printings, and step 2 of the harness blanks every price VALUE — so `null` and `"5950.00"` reduce to the same byte and the byte comparison is blind to it. So is volatile-shape.ts: the key set still matches (check 1), a coalesced value is still a decimal string (check 2), and the run-level counter would go UP rather than dark (check 4). `price_nullity` is the assertion that sees it — the two sides must agree, row for row, about which printings have NO price for these keys, and a case that compares ZERO rows fails rather than passing vacuously. It is opt-in for the same reason check 4 is run-level: one card's foil price appearing between our nightly import and the live API is ordinary churn, and a global nullity check would be red most mornings. tests/routes/price-nullity.test.ts pins that it fires, offline, in both directions.
WHY THIS CARD AND THIS THRESHOLD. A `usd>=` case is a claim about the market unless its membership has room, so the query was chosen for the gap on either side of it: the five rows sit at $1,772.97 and up, and the next Traveling Chocobo printing down is `fin/568` at $125.09. Every matching price would have to fall 44%, or a non-matching one rise 8x, before the answer moves.
WHY NOT `usd>=500 unique=prints`, WHICH IS THE QUERY THIS CASE WAS ASKED FOR. Measured 2026-08-17 across both pages of both sides: api.scryfall.com 254 printings, this port 255, and the extra row is `7ed/218★` Shivan Dragon at a `usd_foil` of exactly `"500.00"` — a corpus-wide threshold sits on somebody's price every day, so that case is green or red depending on where one printing sat when the two snapshots were taken. It is not wasted, though: it is where the population was measured. Over the 254 rows both sides return, `usd` nullity disagrees on ZERO and 144 of them serve `usd: null` while matching `usd>=500`. Those 144 are what a stored-column coalesce corrupts, and the five rows here are five of them.
(`!"Cavern of Souls" usd>=1000` was the first candidate and was rejected for a reason worth recording: `lci/410a` carries `mtgo_id` 117656 on api.scryfall.com and 117666 in Scryfall's own bulk dump, which is what this store is built from — checked in store-build/rows.jsonl. Not our divergence and not this case's subject, but it is red, and its siblings 410b-410e run 117658, 117660, 117662, 117664, so the API's value is the one that fits the run.)
THE ETCHED LEG IS NOT HERE and is not missing by oversight: no etched-only printing in the corpus reaches $500, the highest being `sld/1072` Mox Opal at $381.19, so no threshold that is safe from drift also reaches an etched row. `Mox Opal sld` (usd null, foil null, etched 381.19, matches `usd>=300`) and `Force of Negation h1r` (usd null, foil 113.66, etched 67.45, matches `usd>=100` and would not if etched won the chain) are measured in 417bed6 and pinned by card_engine's own tests, which do not depend on a live price.

known_deviation.reason:
A SCRYFALL BEHAVIOUR NOBODY HERE HAD MEASURED, RECORDED SO IT IS NOT REDISCOVERED AS A SORT BUG. Adding `order=usd` to a query — changing nothing else — CHANGES SCRYFALL'S RESULT SET, and only in the `unique=cards` space. Measured 2026-08-17, four requests:
  `usd>=500`                   205 cards      `order=usd usd>=500`                  35 cards
  `usd>=500 unique=prints`     254 printings  `order=usd usd>=500 unique=prints`   254 printings
The 35 that survive `order=usd` all carry a real `prices.usd`; the 170 that vanish are the cards whose representative printing serves `"usd": null` and matched only through the foil/etched fallback. Under `unique=prints` nothing is dropped and the fallback still ORDERS the page — Scryfall's own first row there is `ltc/392z` at `usd` null with a $10,000.00 foil. So the fallback is in Scryfall's sort key, and the drop is specific to the per-card DISTINCT step: `order=usd` appears to re-decide membership against the representative's raw column rather than the coalesced one.
THIS CASE IS THE MINIMAL WITNESS, and its control is the case above it. `!"Traveling Chocobo" usd>=1000 unique=prints` answers 200 with the same five printings on both sides, byte-clean — that is search-usd-coalesce-is-on-the-search-key-not-the-column. Add `order=usd` and drop to the default `unique=cards`, changing nothing else, and api.scryfall.com answers 404 `not_found`: a query it had just matched five ways now matches nothing, because every one of those five serves `"usd": null`. This port answers the one card.
WHY IT IS RECORDED AND NOT MATCHED. 417bed6 put the coalesce on the search key in all four places on purpose so the filter, the range index and the sort key cannot disagree; reproducing this would mean making `order=usd` re-filter against a DIFFERENT key from the one the planner narrowed with, which is the exact class of bug that commit's index/filter equality test exists to prevent. A caller who sorts by price and loses the rows they filtered for is not being served better by our copying it.
WHAT EACH SIDE IS HELD TO. The STATUS, and on our side the one row and the fact that its `usd` is null — deliberately NOT which printing it is. All five candidates are null-`usd`, so the `usd: null` recording holds whichever one wins, but the representative pick under `order=usd` is the CHEAPEST of them and the two cheapest are $1,772.97 and $1,790.64, one percent apart; recording `551b` would make this case a bet on that gap. The membership behind it has room, though: the five sit at $1,772.97 and up against a $1,000.00 threshold, and the next printing down is $125.09. If api.scryfall.com ever answers 200 here, they have stopped dropping null-priced representatives and this case should be re-measured, not re-recorded.

cases.note: x59, reported from mtg-seeker 2026-10-03: the port refused the whole query (`400 Failed to parse query`) where Scryfall documents the word. ARITHMETIC IN A NUMERIC TERM IS UPSTREAM'S EXTENSION, NOT SCRYFALL SYNTAX, and this is its recorded witness on the compat surface. Measured 2026-10-03: api.scryfall.com answers `pow+tou<6`, `pow+tou=4`, `cmc+1<pow`, `tou*2<pow` and this query with a plain 404 `not_found` and no `warnings` key — the expression is not an error there, it simply matches nothing — while this port evaluates it (3,548 cards that day; the count is not recorded here because it moves with the corpus). It is kept for the reason the regexes on extra columns are kept: answering where Scryfall answers nothing costs a searcher nothing, and `/search` shares the parser.
IT IS NOT A SYNONYM FOR `pt`. Scryfall's own keyword for the sum is `pt`/`powtou` (the four cases above), and the two differ on multi-face cards: `pt` is the FRONT face's power plus toughness, `pow+tou` the existential cross product `pow` and `tou` are each compared over. On Delver of Secrets // Insectile Aberration (1/1 // 3/2) `pt=2` is 1 and `pt=5`, `pt=3`, `pt=4` are 404 on Scryfall; `pow+tou` here answers all four. A client that wants Scryfall's answer writes `pt`.
WHAT EACH SIDE IS HELD TO: the status and the envelope's object only. If api.scryfall.com ever answers 200 here it has grown arithmetic, and this case should be re-measured against it rather than re-recorded.

cases.name: search-negated-class-stops-at-a-line-break
cases.note:
x61, reported from mtg-seeker 2026-10-03: a NEGATED character class matched across a line break here and does not on Scryfall. This query is 1 card on api.scryfall.com — Amulet of Vigor — and was 2 here, the second being Tiller Engine, whose text is "Whenever a land you control enters tapped, choose one —
• Untap that land.
• Tap target nonland permanent an opponent controls.": `[^.]*` ran from the trigger line into the first bullet. The rule is PostgreSQL ARE's newline-sensitive mode, of which this port already had two legs (`.` stops at a newline, `^`/`$` are line anchors) and not the third: a bracket expression using `^` never matches a newline. The engine now writes the newline into every negated class before compiling (`[^.]` becomes `[^
.]`), which keeps the pattern on the linear regex engine and its trigram narrow.

known_deviation.reason: mtg-seeker report R35 (2026-10-04), NOT FIXED — recorded. The report's query ends `o:"perpetually gains \"Whenever" o:"return this card from your graveyard"`: Scryfall 3 cards, this port 5 (Forgeborn Phoenix and Kami of Mourning extra, both through that last pair of terms). The cause is not which text is searched. api.scryfall.com has NO backslash escape inside a quoted string: the phrase ends at the next quote character, so the first term is the phrase `perpetually gains \` — a literal backslash no oracle text holds — and what follows (`Whenever`, then a quoted ` o:`, then bare words) are name terms that match nothing. This port's lexer follows upstream #905, where `\"` is an escaped quote inside the phrase, so the same text is the phrase `perpetually gains "whenever` and matches. Measured 2026-10-04 scoped to Kami of Mourning ("…perpetually gains \"Whenever a creature you control…\""): this case, the backslash form, is 404 on Scryfall and 1 here; the single-quoted spelling `o:'perpetually gains "Whenever'` is 1 on both; `o:"gains \""` is 404 there; an unclosed `o:"whenever` is 1 there (not measured here). Left alone because the fix is the shared lexer's quote rule (src/parser/tokenizer.ts and vendor hand_parser.py, pinned to agree by fixtures, and upstream-compatible on `/search`), which is outside x65's text-semantics scope: it needs a Scryfall-route-only reading of quotes, and a decision about unclosed quotes with it.

known_deviation.reason: THE RESIDUE OF x66's "too complex" rule: a pattern Scryfall runs and this engine's own static budget (parser/regex-budget.ts, upstream #1047) does not. Five lookarounds cost 15 of Scryfall's 90 and run there — 152 instants on api.scryfall.com 2026-10-03 — while the engine admits four. The port used to answer `400 Search query contains an unsupported regular expression.` for the whole query; it now drops the one term with Scryfall's own sentence and answers the rest, so the FAILURE MODE is Scryfall's even though the threshold is not. The same holds for more than 64 constructs (Scryfall runs 89 dots or 82 `\w`), an open-ended `{m,}` with m over 1, and a pattern over 256 UTF-8 bytes that is under 248 characters. It is the safe direction for a client that validates here and ships to Scryfall: the port refuses loudly what Scryfall would have run, never the reverse. Raising the engine's bound is a cost decision — every lookaround pattern scans the corpus on the backtracking engine.

cases.note: 2026-10-09. 404: no variation leads a rarity (38,945 with variations and without). The same 404 for new:card, new:mtgo, new:arena, new:game and new:nonfoil.

cases.name: new-language-holds-no-variation
cases.note: 2026-10-09. 404 over every language: each variation's plain twin of the same day leads its language (285,762 with variations and without).

cases.name: is-misprint-holds-its-variations
cases.note: 2026-10-09, generation 88. 36 rows: m20/206†, mkm/310†, Fifth Edition's five, Final Fantasy's four, ody/72† in English and Japanese, the Spanish mir/87†, the Russian ptor/67† and 67†a … The lists had been read without include_variations=true, which hides every one of them; the port answered a 404.

cases.name: is-misprint-variation-in-two-languages
cases.note: 2026-10-09. ody/72† in English and in Japanese — a collector number in every language it has — and not the plain ody/72. The port answered a 404.

cases.name: is-misprint-variation-hidden-by-default
cases.note: 2026-10-09. 404 by default: the card's one misprint is the variation m20/206†, which the search's own default hides. With include_variations=true it is that row.

cases.name: not-misprint-among-variations
cases.note: 2026-10-09. 86 of the 122 variation rows: Portal's 35, Arabian Nights' 14, ten of Murders at Karlov Manor's eleven … The port answered all 122.

cases.name: is-covered-among-variations
cases.note: 2026-10-09. 46 rows, ph18/4† among them (Heroes of the Realm 2018 is covered whole) and NOT iko/275y, mid/57† or om1/117†. The port answered 48: the four rows were tagged by the tier rule, the variations having been skipped as rows no search returns.

cases.name: not-covered-among-variations
cases.note: 2026-10-09. 76 rows, every one English: the Arena-only iko/275y and mid/57† and Through the Omenpaths' om1/117† are in their cards' first run. The port answered 74.

cases.name: print-order-a-variation-in-the-default-tier
cases.note: 2026-10-09, generation 89. cmm/366, iko/275y, cmm/599, iko/275: the Arena-only variation iko/275y (2022) is in the card's first run — `-is:covered` holds it — ahead of Commander Masters' borderless printing of 2023. The port ranked it by the tier rule alone, which calls an Arena-only printing second-tier, and answered cmm/366, cmm/599, iko/275y, iko/275.

cases.name: unique-cards-answers-a-default-tier-variation
cases.note: 2026-10-09. iko/275y, not the buy-a-box Godzilla printing iko/275 of two years earlier: the first of the card's own order that the filter keeps.

cases.name: print-order-a-variation-beside-its-twin
cases.note: 2026-10-09. mid/57, mid/57†, prm/93940, dbl/57, pmid/57p, pmid/57s, mid/335. The port answered mid/57† sixth, after the prerelease promo.

cases.name: print-order-a-default-tier-variation-before-its-second-tier-twin
cases.note: 2026-10-09. spm/119, om1/117†, om1/117: Through the Omenpaths' plain printings are second-tier and this variation of one is not. The port answered om1/117 before om1/117†.

cases.name: print-order-a-printing-that-departs-from-its-sets-tier
cases.note: 2026-10-09. m3c/315, lcc/317 — the one default-tier printing of Modern Horizons 3 Commander and the one second-tier printing of Lost Caverns Commander, which `-is:covered` and `is:covered` say by name. Not variations: the same record, read for the rank. The port answered lcc/317 first.

cases.name: unique-art-among-variations
cases.note: 2026-10-09, generation 90. 90 artworks, Vizzerdrix's by 9ed/S7a (2005) and not 8ed/S5a (2003): the artwork debuted in 7th Edition, which the query does not match, and with the debut out of scope the answer is the first of the card's own order, not the oldest row left. The port answered 8ed/S5a.

cases.name: unique-art-debut-out-of-scope-answers-the-cards-order
cases.note: 2026-10-09. 9ed/S7 and s99/59. Six printings share the first artwork and the two of 7th Edition, its debut, are filtered away: 9ed/S7 leads the card's own order; 8ed/S5 is the oldest left.

cases.name: unique-art-debut-day-without-the-new-art-row
cases.note: 2026-10-09. 7ed/110 and s99/59. `new:art` names the foil 7ed/110★, which this query drops; the plain 7ed/110 of the same day still represents the artwork over the 8th and 9th Edition printings ahead of it in the card's order.

cases.name: unique-art-reprints-without-the-original
cases.note: 2026-10-09. ima/117 (2017-11), not mm3/89 (2017-03): two reprints of a Rise of the Eldrazi painting, and the newer leads the card's order. The port answered mm3/89, the oldest in scope; 47 of 47 such artworks across `e:vma or e:ema or e:ima or e:mm3` go this way.

cases.name: unique-art-magic-online-reprints
cases.note: 2026-10-09. tpr/15 (2015), not vma/28 (2014). The port answered vma/28; 53 of 53 across six Magic Online sets go this way.

cases.name: unique-art-debut-in-scope-still-answers-it
cases.note: 2026-10-09. ema/65 (2016), not ima/69 (2017): this painting debuted in Eternal Masters, so the older printing answers — the one artwork of 48 in the four masters sets that keeps its oldest, and the reason the key is the debut and not the newest.
